o: They are careless in God's institutions.
bg: Messenger or angel, the last of the minor prophets, and the writer of the last book of the Old Testament canon (Mal. 4:4, 5, 6). Nothing is known of him beyond what is contained in his book of prophecies.

There are many prophecies concerning Edom (Isa. 34:5, 6; Jer. 49:7-18; Ezek. 25:13; 35:1-15; Joel 3:19; Amos 1:11; Obad.; Mal. 1:3, 4) which have been remarkably fulfilled. The present desolate condition of that land is a standing testimony to the inspiration of these prophecies.

Messenger or angel, the last of the minor prophets, and the writer of the last book of the Old Testament canon (Mal. 4:4, 5, 6). Nothing is known of him beyond what is contained in his book of prophecies.
ch.s: This chapter covers: The ingratitude of Israel (vv. 1–5); They are careless in God's institutions (vv. 6–14). People named: Esau, Jacob, Malachi. Places: Edom.
ch.mh: All advantages, either as to outward circumstances, or spiritual privileges, come from the free love of God, who makes one to differ from another.
q: Read verses 1–5 (The ingratitude of Israel). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 6–14 (They are careless in God's institutions), what do you learn about sacrifice and atonement?
Verse 6 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Luke 6:46. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Esau’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of love in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Malachi?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: We may rely on God's mercy for pardon as to the past, but not for indulgence to sin in future.
ch.a: Do one concrete, unannounced act of love for someone in your home or church.

o: The priests reproved for neglecting their covenant.
The people reproved for their evil practices.
bg: Messenger or angel, the last of the minor prophets, and the writer of the last book of the Old Testament canon (Mal. 4:4, 5, 6). Nothing is known of him beyond what is contained in his book of prophecies.
ch.s: This chapter covers: The priests reproved for neglecting their covenant (vv. 1–9); The people reproved for their evil practices (vv. 10–17). People named: Levi, Jacob. Places: Judah, Jerusalem.
ch.mh: What is here said of the covenant of priesthood, is true of the covenant of grace made with all believers, as spiritual priests.
q: Read verses 1–9 (The priests reproved for neglecting their covenant). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 10–17 (The people reproved for their evil practices), what do you learn about covenant?
Verse 7 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside 2 Timothy 2:24–25. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Levi’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of law and instruction in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Malachi?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: We must not only consult the written word, but desire instruction and advice from God's messengers, in the affairs of our souls.
ch.a: Ask God to search your heart, confess what He shows you, and make any right amends.

o: The Jews reproved for their corruptions.
God's care of his people; The distinction between the righteous and the wicked.
bg: Messenger or angel, the last of the minor prophets, and the writer of the last book of the Old Testament canon (Mal. 4:4, 5, 6). Nothing is known of him beyond what is contained in his book of prophecies.
ch.s: This chapter covers: The coming of Christ (vv. 1–6); The Jews reproved for their corruptions (vv. 7–12); God's care of his people; The distinction between the righteous and the wicked (vv. 13–18). People named: Levi, Jacob. Places: Judah, Jerusalem.
ch.mh: The first words of this chapter seem an answer to the scoffers of those days.
q: Read verses 1–6 (The coming of Christ). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 7–12 (The Jews reproved for their corruptions), what do you learn about hope and restoration?
Verse 6 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Numbers 23:19. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Levi’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of family and generations in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Malachi?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: As to ourselves, we have need to think among which we shall have our lot; and, as to others, we must judge nothing before the time.
ch.a: Encourage someone who is discouraged with a promise from this chapter.

bg: Messenger or angel, the last of the minor prophets, and the writer of the last book of the Old Testament canon (Mal. 4:4, 5, 6). Nothing is known of him beyond what is contained in his book of prophecies.

(my God is Jehovah) has been well entitled "the grandest and the most romantic character that Israel ever produced." "Elijah the Tishbite,... of the inhabitants of Gilead" is literally all that is given us to know of his parentage and locality.
ch.s: This chapter covers: The judgements on the wicked, and the happiness of the righteous (vv. 1–3); Regard to be had to the law; John the Baptist promised as the forerunner of Messiah (vv. 4–6). People named: Moses, Horeb, Elijah.
ch.mh: Here is a reference to the first and to the second coming of Christ: God has fixed the day of both.
q: Read verses 1–3 (The judgements on the wicked, and the happiness of the righteous). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 4–6 (Regard to be had to the law; John the Baptist promised as the forerunner of Messiah), what do you learn about law and instruction?
Verse 2 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Jeremiah 33:6. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Moses’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of family and generations in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Malachi?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let others boast in their proud reasoning, and call it enlightening, but let us keep near to that sacred word, through which this Sun of Righteousness shines upon the souls of his people.
ch.a: Memorize the key verse and come back to it each morning this week.
